title: CRA's new pre-filled tax return: set up your account by October 31
description: About one million Canadians will be invited to file a pre-filled 2026 return in March 2027. To qualify, your CRA account must be set up by October 31, 2026.
body_html:
The Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) is launching a free service that fills in your tax return for you using information it already has. Starting in March 2027, about one million Canadians will be invited to use it for their 2026 return. To be considered, you need to have your CRA account set up by October 31, 2026.

What is a pre-filled return?

The CRA already receives most of the slips that simple returns need, such as your T4 from your employer or your pension slips. With the new service, the CRA puts that information into a return for you. You sign in, check everything, add anything that's missing, and then accept and submit it.

It isn't automatic filing. Nothing is filed until you review and submit the return yourself, and you stay responsible for making sure it's correct.

Who may be invited

The first round is aimed at people with lower incomes and simple tax situations who don't owe tax. According to the CRA, you must meet all of these conditions:

  • You have a CRA account, and your correspondence preference is set to electronic mail.
  • You filed your 2025 tax return.
  • You were a Canadian resident for tax purposes for all of 2026, you're filing for yourself, and you were 15 or older in 2026.
  • Your income comes only from certain slips, such as T4, T4A, T4A(OAS), T4A(P), T4E, T5 and T5007, and is below a limit that depends on your province, age and disability tax credit status.

You won't qualify if, in 2026, you sold your principal residence, went bankrupt, repaid COVID-19 benefits or amounts under the Home Buyers' Plan or Lifelong Learning Plan, had exempt income under the Indian Act, or owned specified foreign property costing more than $100,000.

Meeting the conditions doesn't guarantee an invitation. The CRA plans to invite about one million people in 2027 and expand to about 5.5 million by 2029.

What to do by October 31

  1. Sign in to your CRA account, or register if you don't have one.
  2. Check your personal information, including your address and email.
  3. Set your correspondence preference to electronic mail in your account settings.
  4. File your 2025 return if you haven't already. Free options include the CRA's SimpleFile service and community volunteer tax clinics.

If you're invited, you'll get an email in March 2027 telling you the invitation is waiting in your CRA account.

Why filing matters even if you owe nothing

Many benefits are only paid if you file a return every year, including the Canada Child Benefit, the GST/HST credit and several BC credits. A pre-filled return makes it easier for people with simple situations to keep those payments coming.

Is it right for you?

If your only income is from a job or a pension and you have no deductions to claim, a pre-filled return could save you time. But it only includes what the CRA already knows. Credits and deductions that depend on your receipts, such as medical expenses, donations, tuition carry-forwards, moving costs or rent, may be missing unless you add them. If your situation is more than simple, or you're not sure what you can claim, it's worth having your return reviewed.

title: Bank of Canada raises its rate to 2.5%: what it means for you
description: The Bank of Canada raised its policy rate on October 28, 2026, its first increase since 2023, citing higher energy prices and stubborn inflation.
body_html:
On October 28, 2026, the Bank of Canada raised its key interest rate by a quarter of a percentage point, from 2.25% to 2.5%. It's the Bank's first rate increase since July 2023, and it signals that the long run of rate cuts is over for now.

Why the Bank raised rates

Inflation has been higher and has lasted longer than the Bank expected in the summer. Consumer prices have been rising at around 3% a year since April, and the Bank now expects inflation to reach about 3.5% by the end of 2026. High energy prices are the main driver. When gasoline is left out, inflation was a much lower 2.2% in September.

The Bank's concern is that expensive fuel will spread into other prices, as businesses pass on higher transport and production costs. Raising rates now is meant to stop that from turning into a longer bout of inflation.

The economy has also been stronger than expected. It grew at a 3.3% annual pace in the second quarter, and early estimates suggest about 2% in the third. The Bank expects growth of about 1% for 2026 as a whole, with new US tariffs likely to slow things down in the last few months of the year. Unemployment has been around 6.5% for several months.

What it means for you

  • Variable-rate mortgages and lines of credit. Lenders usually move their prime rates in step with the Bank's rate, so borrowing tied to prime generally gets more expensive. Check your lender's notice to see how your payment changes.
  • Fixed-rate mortgages. Your payment won't change until renewal. Fixed rates follow bond yields rather than the Bank's rate directly, and bond yields barely moved on the news.
  • Renewing soon? Compare fixed and variable options carefully, since the Bank has said further increases are possible.
  • Savers. Rates on high-interest savings accounts and GICs may edge up.

What it means for small businesses

Business loans and lines of credit at floating rates will cost a little more. If you carry a balance on a business line of credit, now is a good time to look at your cash flow, pay down expensive debt where you can, and think about how you would handle another increase.

What's next

The Bank said it may need to raise rates further, but will move carefully given the uncertainty around energy prices and trade. Economists at TD expect one more increase in early 2027, which would take the rate to 2.75%. Forecasts like this can change quickly.

The next decision is on December 9, 2026. The Bank's next full economic forecast, the Monetary Policy Report, follows on January 27, 2027.

title: CRA updates for small businesses: online debt payments, Apple Pay and more
description: Business owners can now manage payroll, GST/HST and corporate tax debts online, and pay the CRA with Apple Pay or Google Pay. Here's what's new this fall.
body_html:
The Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) has rolled out several changes this fall that make dealing with it easier for business owners. Here are the ones most likely to matter to small businesses, contractors and corporations.

Manage business tax debts online

Owners, directors and officers can now deal with payroll, GST/HST and corporate (T2) tax balances directly in My Business Account. The new Manage Balance service lets you make a payment, set up a payment arrangement or ask the CRA to call you back, without waiting on the phone. A similar service for personal tax debts launched in October 2025.

One limit to know: accountants and other representatives can't use this service through Represent a Client, so the business owner or a director needs to sign in.

New ways to pay the CRA

Since October 9, 2026, you can pay the CRA with Apple Pay, Google Pay or Konek, as well as by debit card or Interac through participating financial institutions. Whichever way you pay, keep the confirmation with your records.

Keep your director and officer details current

The CRA is reminding corporations to update their records whenever a director or officer joins, leaves or changes their details. Out-of-date information can delay access to My Business Account and stop new representative authorizations from going through.

Rideshare and taxi drivers must register for GST/HST

If you drive for Uber, Lyft or a taxi company, you're generally a self-employed sole proprietor. The CRA's reminder is that rideshare and taxi operators must register for a Business Number and a GST/HST account no matter how much they earn. The usual $30,000 small-supplier threshold doesn't apply to them.

Other changes worth knowing

  • T2 web access code online. Corporations can now get the access code needed to file a T2 return electronically online, without waiting.
  • Faster SR&ED answers. Businesses doing research and development can apply for pre-claim approval, with a decision within eight weeks.
  • Free one-on-one help. The CRA's Liaison Officer Service offers free, confidential visits and sessions for small business owners, self-employed people and landlords.
  • 2027 deadlines. The CRA has published a factsheet of 2027 deadlines for businesses and the self-employed.
  • Extra sign-in security. Individuals and tax preparers can add an optional verification step when filing returns online this coming tax season.

What to do now

  • Make sure you can sign in to My Business Account, and that the right people have access.
  • Check that your directors, officers and addresses are up to date with the CRA.
  • If you owe the CRA and can't pay in full, set up a payment arrangement early. Interest keeps adding up on unpaid balances.
  • Drive for a rideshare platform? Make sure you're registered for GST/HST and charging and remitting it correctly.

sources.title: Businesses tax information newsletter, October 21, 2026 (Canada Revenue Agency)
